topics.title: Room revenue
topics.question: What room revenue follows from your rate and booked nights?
topics.intro: Multiply the room rate by booked nights to model room charges before other receipts or deductions. Keep the nightly-rate definition consistent with the nights being modeled.
topics.limit: This excludes cleaning receipts, guest taxes, refunds and every operating cost. It is not a booking forecast.
topics.action: Compare the modeled room charges with a dated reservation ledger, then reconcile other receipts separately.

topics.title: Booked-night occupancy
topics.question: What share of offered nights is booked?
topics.intro: Divide booked nights by nights offered for booking. Owner use and maintenance closures change the denominator, so availability needs its own evidence.
topics.limit: Values above 100% identify inconsistent inputs; they are not feasible occupancy.
topics.action: Review calendar definitions before comparing your result with another property.

topics.title: Average daily room rate
topics.question: What weighted nightly rate does the room revenue imply?
topics.intro: Dividing room revenue by the booked nights that produced it yields a weighted average rate. This avoids giving a quiet month the same weight as a heavily booked month.
topics.limit: The numerator must exclude receipts that are not room charges for those nights.
topics.action: Check whether the source report includes cleaning charges or taxes in its displayed average.

topics.title: Revenue per available night
topics.question: How much room revenue is earned per offered night?
topics.intro: This calculation spreads room revenue over offered nights, including nights that were available but not booked. It combines the effect of rate and occupancy.
topics.limit: This is not the rate per booked night and does not account for costs.
topics.action: Use the same reporting period for room revenue and available nights.

topics.title: Operating margin
topics.question: What share of room revenue remains after operating costs?
topics.intro: Subtract the entered operating costs from room revenue and divide by revenue. The margin describes the cost definition you supply, not a standardized property valuation.
topics.limit: Debt service, income tax and irregular capital work are outside the entered operating-cost amount unless you explicitly include them.
topics.action: List included expenses before comparing margins between properties.

topics.title: Net operating income
topics.question: What income remains before financing?
topics.intro: Operating income subtracts the recurring operating expenses entered from room revenue. It is useful for separating property operations from the financing choice.
topics.limit: Exclude principal and interest from the operating-cost field for this definition. The result is pre-tax and excludes irregular capital work.
topics.action: Reconcile each recurring cost and identify any unpriced line rather than treating it as zero.

topics.title: Debt-adjusted cash flow
topics.question: What remains after operating costs and debt payments?
topics.intro: The worksheet subtracts both operating costs and annual loan payments from room revenue. Showing those components separately helps reveal whether financing consumes the operating surplus.
topics.limit: It does not automatically include income tax, capital expenditures or changes in reserve balances.
topics.action: Compare the result with your actual cash obligations and keep a separate capital-work schedule.

topics.title: Cash-on-cash percentage
topics.question: What return follows from a defined cash investment?
topics.intro: Divide pre-tax cash flow by all cash included in your investment definition. The denominator can include down payment, closing, setup, fees and committed reserves.
topics.limit: The result depends on your cash-flow definition and is not a total investment return.
topics.action: Retain a component schedule for the cash denominator and label the period of cash flow.

topics.title: Operating yield on price
topics.question: What is operating income as a share of purchase price?
topics.intro: This simple yield divides annual operating income before financing by the purchase price. It allows you to separate operating assumptions from the debt structure.
topics.limit: The price denominator excludes transaction and setup costs. This is not an appraisal or market cap-rate recommendation.
topics.action: Use a consistent operating-cost schedule before comparing property yields.

topics.title: Debt-service coverage
topics.question: How does operating income compare with annual debt service?
topics.intro: Divide annual operating income by annual debt service. A value of one means the two entered amounts are equal; below one means operating income is smaller.
topics.limit: Lenders may define qualifying income or expenses differently. This result does not establish loan eligibility.
topics.action: Ask the lender which income definition and test period its own underwriting uses.

topics.title: Monthly mortgage payment
topics.question: What is the modeled monthly principal and interest payment?
topics.intro: This model uses a fixed annual interest rate and equal monthly payments over the amortization term. At zero interest it divides principal equally across months.
topics.limit: Taxes, insurance, loan fees, mortgage insurance, balloons and variable-rate changes are excluded.
topics.action: Reconcile the illustration with a current lender payment schedule.

topics.title: Annual mortgage payments
topics.question: How much principal and interest is modeled across twelve months?
topics.intro: Multiply the modeled level monthly principal-and-interest payment by twelve. This makes it comparable with an annual operating scenario.
topics.limit: A first partial year, interest-only period or payment change will require a different schedule.
topics.action: Keep the start date and payment type beside the annual amount.

topics.title: Interest-only payment
topics.question: What is one monthly interest-only payment at a fixed rate?
topics.intro: Multiply principal by the annual rate and divide by twelve. The calculation pays no principal and is intentionally different from an amortizing loan model.
topics.limit: Actual day-count conventions, fees and later amortization or maturity terms are not modeled.
topics.action: Identify the length of the interest-only period and the obligations that follow it.

topics.title: Total entry cash
topics.question: What cash is allocated to the purchase and launch?
topics.intro: Add separately defined purchase and launch cash buckets. A reserve allocation is shown as committed cash even though it may remain in an account.
topics.limit: Do not count deposits or costs already included in another bucket twice. This is not a settlement statement.
topics.action: Reconcile every bucket to its source and identify credits or financed amounts separately.

topics.title: Loan-to-price ratio
topics.question: What share of purchase price is represented by the loan?
topics.intro: The ratio divides the entered loan principal by the purchase price. It describes leverage against that price without assuming an appraised value.
topics.limit: A lender may use an appraised value, other basis or different loan amount. This calculation does not establish permitted leverage.
topics.action: Record whether the compared ratio uses price, value or total cost as its denominator.

topics.title: Loan-to-total-cost ratio
topics.question: What share of entered project cost is financed?
topics.intro: Divide principal by the combined project-cost basis you enter. This separates a total-cost ratio from a purchase-price ratio.
topics.limit: Define what belongs in total cost; financing eligibility can use different components.
topics.action: List the project-cost denominator before comparing it with a lender term.

topics.title: Break-even booked nights
topics.question: How many booked nights cover annual fixed costs?
topics.intro: Each booked night contributes the rate less the selected variable percentage. Divide fixed annual costs by that contribution and round up to a whole booked night.
topics.limit: The model assumes a constant contribution per night and does not verify that the required nights can be booked.
topics.action: Compare the result with actual availability and avoid counting fixed costs again in the variable share.

topics.title: Required nightly room rate
topics.question: What rate covers costs at a chosen number of booked nights?
topics.intro: Spread fixed costs across the selected booked nights, then allow for the variable expense percentage. The result is a mathematical cost-covering rate.
topics.limit: Market demand may not support this rate. Minimum stays, discounts and booking changes are not modeled.
topics.action: Treat the result as a question for your revenue evidence, not a pricing recommendation.

topics.title: Variable expense amount
topics.question: What annual cost follows from a revenue percentage?
topics.intro: Apply a selected percentage to the revenue base. The dollar result makes a percentage assumption visible in the operating-cost schedule.
topics.limit: The model does not decide which expenses truly move with revenue or which base a contract uses.
topics.action: Confirm the fee base and distinguish revenue-linked costs from fixed annual obligations.

topics.title: Management fee illustration
topics.question: What management charge follows from an agreed revenue base?
topics.intro: A management percentage only has meaning when its revenue base is defined. This illustration multiplies your chosen base by the fee percentage.
topics.limit: Minimum charges, additional services, taxes and contract exclusions are not incorporated.
topics.action: Compare the result with a sample invoice under the actual management agreement.

topics.title: Blended platform fee
topics.question: What is the combined cost across two booking channels?
topics.intro: Calculate each channel’s charge from its own assumed revenue and percentage, then add the charges. This avoids applying a single rate to a mixed channel portfolio.
topics.limit: Fees are hypothetical inputs, not current platform pricing. Other payment or guest charges are excluded.
topics.action: Verify each platform’s current applicable terms and keep consistent revenue definitions.

topics.title: Turnover contribution
topics.question: What remains from cleaning receipts after cleaner costs?
topics.intro: Multiply the difference between the guest cleaning charge and cleaner cost by the stay count. Negative results identify a modeled turnover shortfall.
topics.limit: Linen replacement, deep cleans, platform charges and tax treatment are not included.
topics.action: Keep per-stay costs separate from costs charged per night or per visit.

topics.title: Annual utility allowance
topics.question: What annual allowance follows from a monthly amount?
topics.intro: Multiply a monthly allowance by the number of included months. This is useful for showing a consistent cost assumption in an annual model.
topics.limit: A level allowance does not model weather, guest use, seasonal tariffs or service changes.
topics.action: Compare the flat assumption with a month-by-month bill schedule.

topics.title: Monthly tax and insurance allowance
topics.question: How much is the monthly equivalent of entered annual amounts?
topics.intro: Add the annual property-tax and insurance assumptions and divide by twelve for a monthly planning amount.
topics.limit: This does not calculate tax liability, premiums, escrow requirements or coverage. Inputs require current property-specific evidence.
topics.action: Use authority records and insurer quotes appropriate to the proposed purchase and use.

topics.title: Replacement reserve allowance
topics.question: What annual allowance follows from replacement cost and interval?
topics.intro: Spread a hypothetical replacement cost evenly across a selected interval. This shows one possible budgeting allowance rather than predicting equipment failure.
topics.limit: Timing, inflation, existing condition and repair alternatives are not included. It is not a tax-depreciation calculation.
topics.action: Keep specialist condition findings separate from your chosen reserve interval.

topics.title: Cash shortfall runway
topics.question: How long could a reserve cover a constant monthly shortfall?
topics.intro: Divide usable reserve by the assumed monthly cash deficit. Funds earmarked for unrelated obligations should not be included as usable reserve.
topics.limit: The shortfall is held constant and there is no replenishment or emergency capital expense.
topics.action: Stress both the size and duration of the shortfall; this result does not recommend a reserve level.

topics.title: Setup cost overrun
topics.question: How much does a selected overrun add to setup cash?
topics.intro: Apply an overrun percentage to the original setup allowance. The result is additional cash rather than the revised full setup total.
topics.limit: The percentage is a scenario choice and does not replace itemized vendor quotes.
topics.action: Identify which unpriced scope items could use the additional allowance.

topics.title: Lost-booking contribution
topics.question: How much contribution is lost when booked nights fall?
topics.intro: Multiply lost room revenue by the share remaining after costs assumed to be avoided. Fixed costs are left unchanged.
topics.limit: Some expenses may not fall immediately when bookings decline. This does not model cancellations or refunds separately.
topics.action: State which costs can actually be avoided and how quickly they change.

topics.title: Nightly-rate sensitivity
topics.question: What is the annual revenue effect of a dollar rate change?
topics.intro: Hold booked nights constant and multiply by a dollar change in the nightly rate. This isolates the arithmetic rate effect.
topics.limit: Changing price can also change bookings, fees and guest mix. Those effects are outside this single-variable model.
topics.action: Follow with a combined rate-and-night scenario before treating the result as a complete view.

topics.title: Room revenue downside
topics.question: What room revenue remains after a percentage reduction?
topics.intro: Apply one total reduction to the base room-revenue assumption. This is an aggregate scenario rather than a model of individual bookings.
topics.limit: It does not identify whether the decline comes from price, occupancy, refunds or availability.
topics.action: Record the cause behind your reduction when deciding which operating costs might also change.

topics.title: Operating cost increase
topics.question: What annual cost follows from an expense increase?
topics.intro: Increase the entered operating-cost total by a selected percentage. This makes an aggregate expense sensitivity visible.
topics.limit: Different expenses can move independently and some are fixed for a period. A single percentage simplifies that detail.
topics.action: Use itemized quotes when a particular cost is large enough to drive the decision.

topics.title: Combined operating stress
topics.question: What cash flow remains when rate, nights and costs all change?
topics.intro: Reduce rate and booked nights multiplicatively, increase operating costs, and retain the debt payment. This tests several connected assumptions together.
topics.limit: This is not a probability estimate. Costs are treated as an annual aggregate, not a booking-sensitive schedule.
topics.action: Write why each stress assumption is plausible for your own scenario without presenting it as a forecast.

topics.title: Two-season room revenue
topics.question: What revenue follows from two different seasonal rates?
topics.intro: Calculate room revenue separately for two seasonal segments and add the results. This avoids applying a peak rate to all booked nights.
topics.limit: Two segments simplify a full calendar and do not validate demand or available inventory.
topics.action: Choose segments whose periods do not overlap and confirm the combined booked nights fit the year.

topics.title: Three-period cash flow
topics.question: What does a three-period cash schedule add up to?
topics.intro: Add net cash results across three non-overlapping periods. Negative entries remain visible rather than being excluded from a favorable total.
topics.limit: The periods must use the same cash-flow definition and together cover the interval you intend to describe.
topics.action: Inspect each period’s funding need even when their combined total is positive.

topics.title: Discounted room rate
topics.question: What nightly rate follows from a simple percentage discount?
topics.intro: Reduce the entered room rate by one percentage discount. This shows the resulting rate before fees, taxes or other adjustments.
topics.limit: Multiple stacked discounts and platform-specific rounding rules are not modeled.
topics.action: Compare the discounted rate with your contribution and cost-covering rate.

topics.title: Simple cash payback
topics.question: How many years of a constant cash flow equal the cash investment?
topics.intro: Divide the cash investment by a constant positive annual cash flow. This is a simple undiscounted payback period.
topics.limit: It ignores time value, mortgage balance, sale proceeds, changing cash flows and tax effects. It is not a total-return model.
topics.action: Use it only as a clearly labeled simplification alongside more complete purchase analysis.

topics.title: Amenity payback illustration
topics.question: How many years of incremental contribution recover an upfront cost?
topics.intro: Divide the upfront cost by assumed incremental revenue less incremental operating cost. This isolates the improvement rather than the whole property’s revenue.
topics.limit: A zero or negative contribution has no finite positive payback. Incremental demand is an assumption, not an established result.
topics.action: Ask what evidence supports incremental bookings and include ongoing servicing costs.

topics.title: Per-night contribution
topics.question: What remains from a booked night after variable cost?
topics.intro: Subtract the entered variable dollar cost from the room rate. The difference contributes toward fixed expenses and any surplus.
topics.limit: A flat cost per night can misstate costs that occur per stay or as a percentage of revenue.
topics.action: Separate turnover frequency from booked-night volume before using this contribution in a break-even model.

topics.title: Owner-use revenue opportunity
topics.question: What gross room revenue corresponds to selected owner-use nights?
topics.intro: Multiply selected owner-use nights by a hypothetical achievable rate. This illustrates gross revenue opportunity rather than a cost charged to the owner.
topics.limit: It assumes those nights could otherwise have been booked and does not subtract avoided operating costs.
topics.action: Use the relevant seasonal rate rather than applying an annual average to every owner stay.

topics.title: Debt payment cushion
topics.question: How much operating income remains above annual debt payments?
topics.intro: Subtract annual debt service from operating income to express the debt cushion in dollars. This complements a coverage ratio when the scale of the margin matters.
topics.limit: A positive cushion does not include every capital, reserve or tax obligation and is not lender approval.
topics.action: Compare the dollar cushion with a combined operating stress rather than relying on a ratio alone.

references.title: Revenue versus receipts
references.question: Why are revenue and cash receipts different?
references.intro: A booked stay can produce room charges, guest taxes, cleaning charges, refunds and platform deductions. A payout may arrive in a different period.
references.action: Build a bridge between the defined revenue amount and the money received rather than relabeling one as the other.
references.limit: Use the room-revenue model only with its stated numerator.

references.title: Percentage versus percentage points
references.question: How should two rate changes be described?
references.intro: A change from 20% to 25% is five percentage points and a 25% relative increase. These are different measures of the same change.
references.action: Write both the original and revised rate before describing the difference.
references.limit: Confusing the two can materially overstate or understate a cost change.

references.title: Multiplicative stress
references.question: Why do rate and night reductions compound?
references.intro: If price and booked nights both change, the revenue factors multiply. Reducing each by 20% leaves 64% of base revenue.
references.action: Show the two factors separately so a reviewer can reproduce the result.
references.limit: Adding the reductions does not reproduce the combined revenue calculation.

references.title: Fixed versus variable costs
references.question: How should a cost be classified for a model?
references.intro: A fixed cost remains in the scenario when bookings change. A variable cost moves with a defined activity or revenue base.
references.action: Classify the cost for the period and decision being modeled; contracts can include both fixed and variable elements.
references.limit: Do not assume every cost changes at the same speed as revenue.

references.title: Per-stay versus per-night costs
references.question: Why does billing unit affect a projection?
references.intro: Two properties with the same booked nights can have different turnover counts if their lengths of stay differ.
references.action: Retain stay count and booked nights separately when modeling cleaning and consumables.
references.limit: A per-stay charge should not be multiplied by booked nights.

references.title: Cash denominator components
references.question: What belongs in total cash invested?
references.intro: The chosen definition can include down payment, closing, setup, service fees and initial reserves. Consistency matters more than an unexplained label.
references.action: List components and their timing beside the cash-on-cash calculation.
references.limit: Do not compare a down-payment-only return with an all-cash return as if they use one base.

references.title: Zero and negative results
references.question: When should a model say not applicable?
references.intro: A ratio with a zero denominator has no defined finite result. A payback model with nonpositive contribution does not produce a meaningful positive recovery time.
references.action: Preserve the underlying inputs and explain why the output is unavailable.
references.limit: Displaying infinity or a negative recovery period can mislead the reader.

references.title: Rounding policy
references.question: Why retain precision until display?
references.intro: Intermediate rounding can change a final ratio or payment. Calculations should use full numerical precision and round only the displayed result.
references.action: Keep unrounded values internally and state the displayed unit.
references.limit: A rounded dollar output can conceal a small positive or negative difference.

references.title: Annual versus monthly periods
references.question: How do you align a calculation’s units?
references.intro: Annual income divided by monthly debt payments creates a ratio with inconsistent periods. Normalize time units first.
references.action: Label every input with its period and show the conversion used.
references.limit: Multiplying a partial period is a modeling assumption, not recorded annual performance.

references.title: Amortization versus maturity
references.question: Why can the loan schedule need two dates?
references.intro: An amortization term determines a level-payment calculation. Maturity determines when remaining principal may become due.
references.action: Record both terms from the lender before relying on a long amortization illustration.
references.limit: A long amortization period does not guarantee the loan remains outstanding that long.

references.title: Interest-only versus amortizing
references.question: What does a lower initial payment omit?
references.intro: An interest-only payment pays interest without scheduled principal reduction. An amortizing payment combines interest and principal over time.
references.action: Model each period according to the actual structure and flag future changes.
references.limit: Do not extrapolate an initial interest-only payment across the entire holding period.

references.title: NOI versus cash flow
references.question: Where does financing enter the model?
references.intro: Operating income describes revenue after operating costs before financing. Debt-adjusted cash flow then subtracts principal and interest payments.
references.action: Show the bridge rather than using the terms interchangeably.
references.limit: Additional tax, capital and reserve obligations can still sit outside either simplified measure.

references.title: Price versus total project cost
references.question: Why can two leverage ratios differ?
references.intro: A purchase-price denominator excludes some acquisition and launch costs. A total-project-cost denominator includes the components you define.
references.action: Name the basis and retain the component schedule when calculating a ratio.
references.limit: A lender may use a different basis from either worksheet.

references.title: Reserve allocation versus expense
references.question: How does earmarked cash differ from a paid cost?
references.intro: A reserve is cash set aside for a purpose. An expense or capital payment occurs when work or another obligation is paid or recognized under the relevant accounting basis.
references.action: Keep the allocation and later transaction distinct to avoid counting the same amount twice.
references.limit: This is model organization rather than accounting or tax advice.

references.title: Sensitivity versus forecast
references.question: What does changing an input establish?
references.intro: A sensitivity shows what the formula does when an assumption changes. It does not assign a likelihood to the changed condition.
references.action: Describe the scenario and the reason for testing it without calling the output predicted performance.
references.limit: A detailed spreadsheet is still conditional on its inputs.

references.title: Nominal payback limits
references.question: What does simple payback leave out?
references.intro: Simple payback divides cash committed by a constant positive cash flow. It does not discount future receipts or include a terminal sale.
references.action: Use the label simple and undiscounted when presenting the result.
references.limit: Do not use it as a substitute for a full investment-return analysis.

references.title: Expense double counting
references.question: How do you detect duplicate costs?
references.intro: A cleaning cost or reserve may appear both as a line item and inside an aggregate management allowance. The model then subtracts it twice.
references.action: Map each expense to one input bucket and document any aggregate inclusions.
references.limit: A more conservative-looking total can still be an incorrect total.

references.title: Input provenance
references.question: What should accompany a calculator input?
references.intro: A value needs a source, date, unit, period and status such as observed, quoted or assumed. The same number can mean different things under different definitions.
references.action: Retain a non-sensitive source reference beside the scenario you export.
references.limit: The calculator checks arithmetic and ranges, not authenticity.

references.title: Model handoff
references.question: How can someone else reproduce a scenario?
references.intro: Share the model name, input set, units, formula version and limitations. A screenshot of the result alone omits important assumptions.
references.action: Export the browser worksheet and retain it with your source register.
references.limit: An exported file contains your entries; review it before sharing.
